title: First-look: Hosted Gen sandbox + streaming edge-cases
summary: Intro demo of Redwood hosted generation sandbox focused on streaming behavior and several edge cases. Team covered streaming parameters, suggested retry/backoff best practices, prefix caching notes, and an intro to Console metrics. Customer raised SOC 2 / V P C concerns and asked for a short pilot and benchmark sheet. Agreed next steps: send security pack, sample pricing + pilot plan, schedule pilot kickoff and run a 1-run benchmark with customer's 2 prompts.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya, account exec for Redwood Inference. Today Ethan and I will do a short sandbox demo of the hosted generation API with a focus on streaming and some weird edge cases folks hit in prod. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Laura Gomez: Good, thanks. We are excited to see the streaming stuff—latency is big for us, and cost obviously, so wanna see tradeoffs.
[00:14] Daniel Reed: Yeah, and we run mostly on GCP, VPC peering, and we have KMS. We'll want to talk about key management and retention.
[00:21] Ethan Park: Great context. Quick agenda: 1) demo the sandbox call and streaming chunks, 2) parameter walkthrough (temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop), 3) retry and idempotency patterns, 4) observable metrics in Console, 5) Q&A and next steps.
[00:36] Maya Chen: We'll also show how minimal config changes can move latency vs cost. We'll try to keep it interactive.
[00:42] [01:02] Ethan Park: Okay I'm sharing the sandbox link — it's the hosted gen playground in Redwood Console, we have a short prompt sample. Running a chat.gen streaming call now.
[01:12] Speaker 1: (inaudible) yeah go ahead.
[01:15] Ethan Park: You should see token deltas arrive progressively — sandbox uses chunked SSE. You'll notice initial latency is about 120ms from the platform to the first token with our tiny test prompt.
[01:26] Daniel Reed: Is that cold-start or warmed?
[01:29] Ethan Park: This was warmed — prefix was small. Cold-start can add a couple hundred ms depending on model and recent activity. We can pin model versions or Dedicated pools to reduce cold overhead.
[01:38] Laura Gomez: When you say pin model versions is that like forcing a specific quantized variant?
[01:43] Ethan Park: Exactly — you can pin a model artifact and variant. For example q4 vs q8f, and that affects latency and token cost. In the Console we surface lat/throughput columns so you can decide.
[01:54] [02:08] Maya Chen: Quick question for you Laura — what's an SLA or latency target you need for your main user flow?
[02:13] Laura Gomez: Ideally p50 under 200ms and p95 under 700ms for short responses (~60 tokens).
[02:20] Maya Chen: Helpful. We may recommend Dedicated for strict p95, but Hosted often hits p50/p95 good enough for many customers with proper batching and caching.
[02:32] [02:40] Ethan Park: Now let's change parameters. I'll increase temperature to 0.9 and reduce top_p, you'll see the generation becomes less deterministic and streaming pattern slightly different — more micro-tokens at the end.
[02:52] Speaker 2: Sorry, micro tokens?
[02:54] Ethan Park: I mean shorter chunks emitted more frequently; not literally micro tokens. Transcription is weird — sorry.
[02:58] [03:05] Maya Chen: We also want to highlight retry behavior. If a transient network error occurs mid-stream, the recommended approach is to retry with an idempotency key and use the server-provided resume token when available, or rebuild the prompt with last-ok prefix to avoid duplication.
[03:20] Daniel Reed: Can you elaborate on resume token?
[03:23] Ethan Park: Sure. In streaming we can return a minimal resume state — a KV-style last-cursor — that the client can pass on retry so the model can continue without regenerating previously accepted tokens. It's not available for every model variant yet but we surface it when supported.
[03:37] [03:50] Laura Gomez: That sounds helpful. How does that play with our front-end which expects idempotent responses?
[03:54] Ethan Park: Common pattern: client holds idempotency_key and last_confirmed_token_index. On retry, call with idempotency_key plus resume_index. Server either resumes or returns full result if resume not supported. We also show a sample SDK snippet in the repo.
[04:07] [04:22] Maya Chen: Turning to observability — the Console shows per-request token cost, per-route latency histograms, and a token-level cost breakdown. We'll pull that up.
[04:30] Ethan Park: (shares screen) here's a live request timeline. Note the spikes before streaming stop — that's the tokenizer and final sampling step. For long outputs you can see how KV-caching reduces early latency on repeated prefixes.
[04:45] Daniel Reed: We use a lot of repeated prefixes — e.g., reply templates — would caching help a lot?
[04:49] Ethan Park: Yes, prefix/KV cache can shave off ~30-60% of token compute in many workloads, depending on prefix length and cache hit rate. But it's workload dependent.
[05:00] [05:20] Laura Gomez: Security questions — we need SOC 2 plus audit logs, and our legal team will want to understand data retention and whether audio/text is stored.
[05:28] Maya Chen: We have SOC 2 Type II and provide audit logs in Console. For hosted we have configurable retention windows; we also offer Private deployment for full data isolation, or Dedicated with optional no-retention flags per contract. We'll send the security pack.
[05:44] Daniel Reed: KMS — can we bring our own?
[05:47] Ethan Park: Yes, BYOK supported for Private and for Dedicated via customer-managed KMS integrations in the region. Hosted has a managed KMS but we can discuss enterprise options.
[05:56] [06:10] Maya Chen: One edge case I want to demo: network jitter mid-stream. I'll simulate a 2-second pause.
[06:17] Ethan Park: (simulates) pause — client retries after 1.5s with exponential backoff, and server returns resume token. You can see the UI picks up and continues. In cases where resume isn't available, fallback is to re-request with an idempotency key and the client may stitch results or show a grace message.
[06:36] Speaker 3: [inaudible] stitching is messy.
[06:39] Ethan Park: Yes, stitching is messy. We recommend app-level dedupe by token index.
[06:45] [07:00] Maya Chen: Another common question — how do we tune for cost? Two levers: model variant/quantization and batching policy. Increasing batch window reduces per-token cost but raises tail latency; we can set autoscaling and batching thresholds in Dedicated. In Hosted, we provide automated batching heuristics and suggestions in Optimize.
[07:18] Daniel Reed: Can we get rules to auto-fallback to cheaper variants on peak loads?
[07:23] Ethan Park: Yes, Smart routing policies can route to lower-cost variants or regions when latency SLOs allow. We can demo a canary-type config that falls back to q4 variants under heavy load.
[07:36] [07:52] Laura Gomez: We have compliance windows where data must stay in EU. How do we ensure region pinning?
[07:58] Ethan Park: You can pin model routes to regions and we support region affinity in routing policies. For higher compliance you can use Private VPC or Dedicated in specific region. We'll mark this for the pilot.
[08:12] [08:28] Maya Chen: Quick live QA — Priya, any product questions?
[08:31] Priya Nair: Yes, on stop sequences: sometimes models ignore stops mid-stream. Is there a recommended pattern?
[08:38] Ethan Park: Use a combination of stop tokens and shorter max_tokens, and do server-side post-filtering. For streaming, the client should watch for the stop token and gracefully drop subsequent tokens if they arrive. For safety-critical flows, we recommend server-side enforced truncation.
[08:55] [09:10] Speaker 1: Do you have SDK examples for JS and Go for retry logic?
[09:14] Ethan Park: Yes both in our SDKs; we have a small snippet in the sandbox repo showing exponential backoff with jitter, idempotency headers, and resume handling. We'll share the repo link.
[09:25] [09:40] Maya Chen: We're approaching the last 10 minutes. Recap: demoed sandbox streaming, resume token concept, prefix caching benefits, parameter tuning tradeoffs, and Console observability. Next we'll cover pilot scope.
[09:52] Daniel Reed: Pilot idea — run two of our most-used prompts for 48 hours against hosted gen, collect latency and cost, compare to our threshold. Can you run a benchmark sheet?
[10:03] Maya Chen: Absolutely. We'll run a controlled pilot and provide a benchmark spreadsheet. We'll also include a pricing estimate and security pack.
[10:12] Laura Gomez: Timeline — we want results within 2 weeks to decide on Dedicated vs Hosted.
[10:17] Maya Chen: Sounds reasonable. Ethan, anything else?
[10:20] Ethan Park: I'll add an example for handling mid-stream disconnects in the SDK snippet, and a short runbook for when resume isn't available.
[10:28] Priya Nair: Also can you show how Console filters by route and token-cost so product folks can analyze?
[10:33] Ethan Park: Yes we'll export a small demo dashboard and share the view link.
[10:38] [10:45] Maya Chen: Great. Final quick note on competitors: some teams compare us to big cloud endpoints and self-hosted runtimes; we discussed cost/latency tradeoffs.
[10:55] Laura Gomez: Any hard blockers? For legal we'll need data processing addendum and SOC2 report.
[11:01] Maya Chen: We'll send both.
[11:05] Ethan Park: One more practical edge-case: tokenization mismatch. If you pre-tokenize client-side and server uses different tokenizer version you'll see off-by-one. Keep tokenizer versions aligned and use server-side tokenization when possible.
[11:18] Daniel Reed: Good call.
[11:22] Maya Chen: Okay, thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the security pack, pilot plan, pricing, and SDK snippets.
[11:30] Laura Gomez: Thanks, appreciated.
[11:33] Maya Chen: End of demo.
